gamespot.com/articles/why-is-link-the-wo.excerpt: The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake was always going to prove divisive. Personally? I think it looks just fine. I was slightly underwhelmed by the fact that, aside from quality-of-life improvements and an essential modernization of certain gameplay mechanics, Nintendo is pretty much poised to deliver a 1:1 remake. The scale of characters, depth of locations, and overall scope of Link’s world is seemingly identical to the Nintendo 64 original . Monsters might be newly positioned and items could be gained in different ways, but it’s clear that the gameplay experience fans are intimately familiar with is being preserved. For better or worse. Putting gameplay improvements aside though, we need to talk about the visuals. gamespot.com/articles/we-need-to-see-how.excerpt: There's no denying that The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time remake looks weird. Whether you think it skews too far into the direction of realism or you're bawling your eyes out over how good Hyrule looks all these decades later, it's strange to see such a distinct and recognizable game look like this. And I'm hoping that it's received well, because I would love to see the same treatment applied to Ocarina of Time's incredibly strange and dark sequel, The Legend of Zelda: Majora's Mask, if only too see just how messed up that moon is going to look. It's possible you've never played Majora's Mask but will immediately recognize one of its primary antagonists: a menacing and ever-present moon that is slowly hurtling towards Clock Town over the span of three days. As time progresses, its creepy grin edges closer and closer to the ground, a constant reminder of the impending doom that only you can stop. It's a striking design that, alongside the equally iconic design of the titular Majora's Mask, gives such a different look and feel to the majesty of Hyrule in Ocarina of Time. While the Nintendo 3DS remake offered a way to see this menancing moon in more detail, I really can't wait to see what Nintendo can do if it decides to go down the same route as its most recent remake. Young Link has an incredible amount of detail to the point of uncanniness, and that extends to an arresting first look at young Zelda that stood out (to me at least) as the strangest interpretation of the lot. There are many others that look a lot better--adult Link and Sheik look pretty great--but these are all characters that were designed to be friendly and inviting. gamespot.com/articles/xbox-disc-to-digit.excerpt: Xbox's disc-to-digital program looks like it could be a vital step forward for players who want to hold on to their physical games in an increasingly digital world, but it does have limits. Not every game publisher is on board with it, it seems, as Xbox users are reporting that four of the biggest companies aren't "participating" at all. So far, it looks like games from Sega, Square Enix, Ubisoft, and Bandai Namco are largely incompatible with the disc-to-digital service. As verified by Kotaku , popping in a disc for a game from one of those publishers could result in a "not participating in digital licensing" message. What's the reason for this? It could be down to good ol' economics, as the companies would probably prefer that you buy one of their games again on the digital storefront. After all, if you decide to pick up a physical copy of a title from a local secondhand store or through a private sale, they're not seeing a cent of that cash when it changes hands. gamespot.com/articles/gamestop-sets-a-ne.excerpt: Retailer GameStop has released its latest earnings report , and it was a record-breaker for the company. The Texas-based retailer's biggest number for its fiscal Q2 quarter that ended August 1 was $160.2 million. That's how much GameStop made in operating income for the period, and it was the highest Q2 operating income level since the company went public in 2002. Net income was up, too, reaching $298.7 million, compared to $168.6 million last year. GameStop benefitted from continued growth in its biggest sales category--collectibles--which saw net sales jump a whopping 57% year-over-year to $356.3 million. For this latest period, collectibles made up 45.1% of GameStop's net sales. GameStop was once primarily known as a video game retailer, and while it still sells games, consoles, and accessories, the company's biggest revenue-driver today is collectibles. Anyone who has walked into a GameStop store recently can attest to how much shelf space is dedicated to collectibles. GameStop's next-largest revenue-driver was its "video game" category, which reached $263.2 million for the period, down sharply from $494.6 million during the same period last year that benefitted from the Switch 2 launch. Finally, GameStop's pre-owned and refurbished business made up $170.7 million during the period, down from $250 million last year. Some might have thought that Sony's decision to end support for physical game discs, and GTA 6 not releasing on a disc, would be a death knell for a company like GameStop. However, physical video game sales are "irrelevant" to the company , CEO Ryan Cohen has said. He has also suggested GameStop could expand its business into the "live commerce" category that is popular  on TikTok . The executive has also discussed the possibility of GameStop becoming a marketplace for re-selling digital gaming items .
